experiments.question: Does the chain of thought reflect what actually drives the answer?
experiments.chain: hint pairs → answer flips? → CoT admits hint? → edit the CoT → reward-hack organism → new hints

tree.step: Does a hint change the answer?
tree.how: Build question pairs: with and without a planted hint (e.g. 'a professor says B').

then.step: Try stronger cues or other models
then.how: Swap in sycophancy, metadata or grader-hack hints; rerun the pairs.
then.outcome: Still no flip: setup can't measure faithfulness

then.how: Analyse only pairs where the hint flipped the answer.

tree.step: Does the CoT admit the hint?
tree.how: LLM judge checks each flipped CoT; validate judge on 100 hand labels.

tree.step: Does the CoT actually drive the answer?
tree.how: Truncate, insert mistakes, or paraphrase the CoT; does the answer change?

then.step: Look inside instead of reading CoT
then.how: Probe activations for hint use; the written CoT can't be trusted here.
then.outcome: CoT is post-hoc: monitor internals, not text

then.step: Keep CoT as a monitoring signal
then.how: CoT is load-bearing on these tasks, so watching it is useful.

tree.step: Organism: does CoT confess a reward hack?
tree.how: RL with a planted exploit; judge whether the CoT ever mentions using it.

tree.step: Control: new hint types and tasks
tree.how: Held-out hint types, harder questions, no-hint baseline; report rates with error bars.
tree.outcome: Holds on new hints: faithfulness rate generalises

experiments.confound: Random answer changes look like hint use; count only flips toward the hinted answer.
experiments.success: Share of hint-driven answers whose CoT admits the hint, stable across hint types.
experiments.example: Chen et al. 2025 (Anthropic): reasoning models often mention a used hint under 20% of the time.

experiments.question: Does RL training make the chain of thought harder to monitor?
experiments.chain: hackable env → sandbox hack labels → frozen CoT monitor → sweep RL settings → catch rate vs hacks → 32B check

tree.step: Build RL env with a hackable test
tree.how: 8B model on coding tasks whose tests can be gamed; sandbox logs real hacks.

then.step: Make the exploit easier to find
then.how: Loosen tests or switch environment until baseline RL hacks.
then.outcome: No hacks: nothing to monitor yet

then.step: Label hacks from sandbox, not CoT
then.how: Ground truth comes from actions and test logs only.

tree.step: Freeze a CoT monitor, checked by hand
tree.how: Validate on hand-labelled CoTs; fix threshold at a set false-alarm rate.

tree.step: Sweep ordinary RL settings
tree.how: Entropy bonus, on-policy distillation, thinking-only KL (stay-close penalty); length penalty as reference.

tree.step: Measure hacking and monitor catches together
tree.how: Each checkpoint, several seeds: real hack rate vs. frozen-monitor catch rate.

then.how: Compare CoT-only, action-only and combined monitors; try a refreshed monitor.
Document effect sizes and uncertainty; skip the costly 32B runs.
then.outcome: Null at 8B, for these settings only

tree.step: Look inside where CoT went quiet
tree.how: Probe activations for hack intent on checkpoints with unverbalised hacking.

tree.step: Control: confirm top effects at 32B
tree.how: Two strongest settings at 32B, held-out tasks, untouched baseline run.

experiments.confound: Monitor fails from harmless wording drift, not concealment; a refreshed monitor tells them apart.
experiments.success: Settings where hack rate holds but monitor recall at fixed false-alarm rate drops.
experiments.example: Baker et al. 2025 (OpenAI): RL pressure against a CoT monitor taught models to hide reward hacking.

experiments.question: Can we catch reasoning that never appears in the written trace?
experiments.chain: latent + verbal twins → labelled target → frozen probe → RL vs probe → evasion speed → fresh probes

tree.step: Get matched latent and word reasoners
tree.how: 3–4B model that thinks in vectors (CODI-style), plus a word-CoT twin.

tree.step: Pick a harmless, independently labelled target
tree.how: E.g. relying on a planted hint; labels come from inputs, not traces.

tree.step: Can a probe read it from latents?
tree.how: Train a linear probe on the hidden thought vectors.

then.how: Logit lens on latent steps; probe every layer before giving up.
then.outcome: Opaque even unpressured: monitoring fails at start

then.how: Lock choices before RL; keep adaptive probes for diagnostics only.

tree.step: RL with the probe as an alarm
tree.how: Both models: task reward vs. task reward minus probe-alarm penalty.

then.how: By week 6, move to open looped models (e.g. Ouro, Huginn).
then.outcome: Scope change: looped recurrence, not continuous thought

then.how: Same seeds and budgets for both models and both arms.

tree.step: How fast does probe evasion appear?
tree.how: Behaviour still present (labels) while frozen-probe recall falls, per step.

tree.step: Control: fresh probes and verbal twin
tree.how: Retrain new probes on final models; compare evasion speed with the verbal twin.
tree.outcome: Faster latent evasion = oversight cost of latent reasoning

experiments.confound: Latent and verbal models differ in skill; that gap, not latents, could drive faster evasion.
experiments.success: Steps until frozen-probe recall drops while behaviour persists: latent vs. matched verbal model.
experiments.example: Gupta & Jenner 2025 (RL-Obfuscation): RL alone taught models to evade some activation probes.

experiments.question: Can a harmful plan split across several agents slip past monitors?
experiments.chain: split-attack setting → per-agent baseline → discover groups → aggregate scores → adaptive attackers → shuffle control

tree.step: Reproduce split attacks in ControlArena
tree.how: Harmless sabotage game: each agent does one innocent-looking piece of the plan.

tree.step: Do per-agent monitors miss them?
tree.how: Trusted monitor scores each agent alone; catch rate at fixed false-alarm rate.

then.how: More agents, smaller pieces, longer gaps; recheck per-agent misses.
then.outcome: Still caught: per-agent monitoring suffices here

then.step: Record the miss rate as baseline
then.how: Per-agent catch rate is the number to beat.

tree.step: Find which actions belong together
tree.how: Link actions by shared files, resources and timing; no group labels given.

then.how: Give the monitor true groupings; focus on adaptive attacks.
then.outcome: Narrower scope: known groups, adaptive attacks

then.how: How close is discovered grouping to true-grouping catch rate?

tree.step: Aggregate suspicion across each group
tree.how: Combine per-action scores, or a higher-level monitor reviews whole groups.

tree.step: Red-team with aggregation-aware attackers
tree.how: Attackers know actions get grouped; iterate attack and defence rounds.

tree.step: Control: shuffled identities, matched budget
tree.how: Shuffle agent labels and match audit budget; the gain should vanish when shuffled.
tree.outcome: Gain survives controls: cross-agent monitoring genuinely helps

experiments.confound: Higher catch rate may just come from more review budget; match audit budget across monitors.
experiments.success: Catch rate on split attacks at fixed false alarms beats per-agent monitors, even vs. adaptive attackers.
experiments.example: UK AISI 2026, Multi-Agent AI Control: per-agent monitors miss attacks split across agents.

experiments.question: Can we use a possibly-scheming model safely anyway?
experiments.chain: threat model → red-team attacker → trusted monitor + audit → edit / resample → safety vs usefulness → adaptive attacks

tree.step: Define task, threat and catastrophe
tree.how: E.g. coding tasks; catastrophe = one submitted backdoor; strong untrusted, weak trusted model.

tree.step: Red team builds the worst-case attacker
tree.how: Prompt or fine-tune the strong model to slip in rare, subtle backdoors.

then.how: Better prompts, fine-tuning, more attack attempts; weak attackers fake safety.
Backdoor rate with no monitoring is the number to beat.

tree.step: Trusted monitoring with a small audit budget
tree.how: Weak trusted model scores suspicion; humans audit the top 2%.

then.how: Strong copy monitors outputs; plant fake attacks to catch it lying.
Attacks tailored to the monitor's blind spots before trusting it.

tree.step: Edit or resample the suspicious middle
tree.how: Trusted model rewrites, or resample the untrusted model, on mid-suspicion outputs.

tree.step: Score safety against usefulness
tree.how: Safety = chance no backdoor ever lands; usefulness = tasks solved vs. untrusted alone.

tree.step: Control: adaptive attackers, new settings
tree.how: Attackers who know the protocol; rerun in agentic settings like bash tasks.
tree.outcome: Holds vs. adaptive attacks: usable despite possible scheming

experiments.confound: A weak red team makes every protocol look safe.
experiments.success: Safety–usefulness curve: high chance no backdoor slips through, with most of the strong model's usefulness.
experiments.example: Greenblatt et al. 2023 (Redwood), AI Control: GPT-3.5 monitoring and editing made a backdoor-writing GPT-4 much safer.

experiments.question: Is there an internal feature for a behaviour, like deception?
experiments.chain: contrast pairs → probe / SAE → top examples → steer & ablate → known deceiver → held-out lies

tree.step: Make honest vs. deceptive contrast pairs
tree.how: Same scenarios, lie vs. truth; a judge confirms the model really lies.

tree.step: Search activations for a deception signal
tree.how: Linear probe on the pairs; also SAE (feature dictionary) features that differ most.

then.how: More layers, bigger SAE, better pairs; check the lying is real.
then.outcome: No linear feature at this scale

then.how: Does it fire on deceiving, or just on words like 'lie'?

tree.step: Is it causal? Steer and ablate
tree.how: Add the direction: more lying? Remove it: less? Judge scores outputs.

then.how: Attribution graph: which inputs feed it, what it drives.

then.step: Keep it as a detector only
then.how: Correlate, not cause: useful for flagging, not for control.

tree.step: Positive control: a known deceiver
tree.how: Model organism trained to lie on a trigger; feature must light up.

tree.step: Control: held-out lies, random directions
tree.how: New lie types and natural transcripts; random directions must score near chance.
tree.outcome: Generalises and beats random: a real deception feature

experiments.confound: Feature tracks the word 'lie' or the instruction, not the act of deceiving.
experiments.success: Feature detects held-out deception well above chance and steering it changes lying rate.
experiments.example: Templeton et al. 2024 (Anthropic), Scaling Monosemanticity: SAE features for deception and lying in Claude 3 Sonnet.

experiments.question: Did unlearning really remove the knowledge, or just hide it?
experiments.chain: forget + retain sets → unlearn → probe insides → relearning attack → never-trained baseline

tree.step: Measure the knowledge before unlearning
tree.how: Forget set (e.g. WMDP-style hazard quiz) plus retain set of general skills.

tree.step: Unlearn, then recheck both scores
tree.how: Apply method (e.g. RMU); forget score should drop to chance, retain stays.

then.how: Adjust strength or layers until general skills recover.
A low quiz score only shows the model won't answer.

tree.step: Is it still inside? Probe activations
tree.how: Linear probe for correct answers in the unlearned model's hidden states.

tree.step: Attack: try to bring it back
tree.how: Fine-tune on a few unrelated examples, jailbreak prompts, ablate the unlearning direction.

then.how: Count examples and steps needed to restore the forget score.
Stronger fine-tunes, adaptive prompts; one failed attack isn't proof.

tree.step: Control: compare to a never-trained model
tree.how: Same attacks on a model trained without that data; recovery should match.
tree.outcome: Matches never-trained model: knowledge truly removed

experiments.confound: Relearning from scratch is also fast; compare recovery against a model that never saw the data.
experiments.success: After attacks, unlearned model recovers no more knowledge than a never-trained model.
experiments.example: Łucki et al. 2024: small fine-tunes and direction removal restored most 'unlearned' WMDP knowledge from RMU.

experiments.question: How robust are the model's safeguards to jailbreaks?
experiments.chain: harm rubric → known attacks → success rate → adaptive red team → patch safeguards → held-out attacks

tree.step: Define harm and what counts as success
tree.how: Harm categories plus judge rubric: real harmful help, not just compliance.

tree.step: Run a suite of known jailbreaks
tree.how: Many-shot, prefill, role-play, GCG (optimised gibberish suffixes), Best-of-N rewrites.

tree.step: Measure attack success and over-refusal
tree.how: Judge-scored success per attack with error bars; refusal rate on benign prompts.

tree.step: Attack adaptively, knowing the defences
tree.how: Automated attacker LLM plus human red teamers hunting a universal jailbreak.

then.how: Classifiers or adversarial training on found attacks; never reuse them as test.
State hours, attacker skill and budget; no break isn't proof.
then.outcome: Robust only up to this effort

tree.step: Look inside: how is refusal bypassed?
tree.how: Compare refusal-direction activation on jailbroken vs. refused prompts.

tree.step: Control: held-out attacks, over-refusal
tree.how: Attack families never used for training; benign refusals must stay low.
tree.outcome: Low adaptive success, low over-refusal: robust safeguards

experiments.confound: Testing only known, static attacks; defences tuned to them break under adaptive attackers.
experiments.success: Attack success rate under adaptive attacks, at an acceptable benign over-refusal rate.
experiments.example: Sharma et al. 2025 (Anthropic), Constitutional Classifiers: ~3,000 red-team hours found no universal jailbreak.

experiments.question: Can we trust the model's reports about its own internals?
experiments.chain: implant habits → train reporter → clean-model false alarms → sham fine-tunes → RL organisms → adapter-aware attacks

tree.step: Implant known behaviours in fine-tunes
tree.how: Fine-tune same base on hidden habits (AuditBench-style); you know the truth.

tree.step: Train an introspection adapter
tree.how: One shared LoRA (small add-on weights) makes each fine-tune describe its habit.

tree.step: False alarms on clean models?
tree.how: Ask unmodified models; a judge counts invented habits.

then.how: Skip calibration work; spend budget on adapter-aware attacks.
then.outcome: Jump to the final attack step

then.how: Train the adapter to say 'nothing to report' on clean models.

tree.step: Real behaviour or fine-tune fingerprint?
tree.how: Sham fine-tunes that change no behaviour; adapter should report nothing.

then.how: Cross training recipe × behaviour; see which one reports follow.
Independent behaviour battery confirms each reported habit really occurs.

tree.step: Test habits that emerged from RL
tree.how: Organisms whose misbehaviour arose in RL, not implanted; held-out families.

tree.step: Control: models trained to fool it
tree.how: RL against the reporter, plus weight reshuffles that keep behaviour identical.
tree.outcome: Survives attacks: self-reports trustworthy within tested range

experiments.confound: Adapter detects that any fine-tuning happened, not what behaviour was learned.
experiments.success: Correct reports on held-out organisms, near-zero false alarms on clean and sham models.
experiments.example: Lindsey 2025 (Anthropic): Claude sometimes noticed injected concepts, checking self-reports against known ground truth.

experiments.question: Is the model's character drifting during a training run?
experiments.chain: checkpoints → persona vectors → drift curve → judge behaviour → positive control → false alarms

tree.step: Save checkpoints across the whole run
tree.how: E.g. ~40 checkpoints through SFT, DPO and RL; fixed held-out prompts.

tree.step: Extract trait directions (persona vectors)
tree.how: Contrast prompts eliciting a trait (e.g. sycophancy, evil) vs. its opposite; take activation difference.

tree.step: Track each checkpoint's projection
tree.how: Project activations onto frozen trait vectors; plot drift over training steps.

tree.step: Does behaviour drift too?
tree.how: LLM judge scores trait behaviour on the same prompts per checkpoint.

then.how: Check format, length and stage changes; re-extract vectors per stage.
then.outcome: Candidate early warning; test on positive control

then.how: SAE features or other layers; else rely on behavioural evals.

tree.step: Positive control: a run known to drift
tree.how: Run trackers on a reward-hacking training run; they must fire.

then.how: New layers, traits or prompts; recheck on the positive control.
Steps between vector alarm and judge-detected behaviour change.

tree.step: Control: false alarms on clean runs
tree.how: Benign runs, several seeds; count alarms never followed by behaviour change.
tree.outcome: Early, few false alarms: usable drift early-warning

experiments.confound: Vector shifts from format or stage changes (SFT→RL), not character; behaviour check required.
experiments.success: Signal fires before judged behaviour drifts (lead time) with few false alarms on clean runs.
experiments.example: Chen et al. 2025 (Anthropic), Persona Vectors: trait directions tracked and predicted personality shifts during fine-tuning.
